data.targetWord: Human life is meaningless

data.sourceWord: Messiah — individual who will come in the future
data.targetWord: Orthodox Jews believe the Messiah is an individual who will come in the future, inaugurate the Messianic Age, rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem, and bring all Jews back to Israel.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.2 — Jewish beliefs about the Messiah

data.sourceWord: Messiah — symbolic concept for Reform Jews
data.targetWord: Reform Jews tend to see the Messiah not as a specific individual but as a symbol of the Messianic Age — a future era of peace and justice that Jews help bring about through their actions.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.2 — Jewish beliefs about the Messiah

data.sourceWord: Messiah — will fulfil prophecies
data.targetWord: According to Maimonides, the Messiah will fulfil specific prophecies: rebuilding the Temple, gathering all Jews to Israel, ushering in an era of universal peace, and bringing all nations to recognise God.

data.sourceWord: Messiah — contrast with Christian belief
data.targetWord: Jews reject the Christian belief that Jesus was the Messiah, because he did not fulfil the key prophecies (rebuilding the Temple, universal peace). For Jews, the Messiah is still awaited.

data.sourceWord: Covenant with Abraham — personal relationship with God
data.targetWord: The Abrahamic covenant was a personal relationship between God and Abraham, initiated by God. Abraham's descendants (the Jewish people) are included in this covenant through circumcision.

data.sourceWord: Covenant with Abraham — land and identity
data.targetWord: God's promise of the land of Canaan to Abraham and his descendants underpins Jewish connection to the Land of Israel. Jews believe this covenant remains active and gives Israel a divine significance.

data.sourceWord: Scripture: God's promise to Abraham
data.targetWord: 'I will make you into a great nation and I will bless you; I will make your name great, and you will be a blessing.' (Genesis 12:2) — the foundational promise of the Abrahamic covenant.

data.sourceWord: FOR: God as Creator gives the best understanding of God
data.targetWord: Belief in God as Creator emphasises his transcendence, omnipotence and care for creation. 'What he created was good and in accordance with his will' — this concept underpins all other beliefs about God.

data.sourceWord: FOR: The Shema expresses the oneness of God most fully
data.targetWord: The Shema — 'Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One' — is the central affirmation of Jewish faith. Belief in God's oneness gives the best understanding of his nature and shapes all other theology.

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: No single concept fully captures God's nature
data.targetWord: No one concept of God gives a complete understanding — God as Creator, Law-Giver, Judge, Redeemer and Shekhinah are all valid and partial perspectives. God's nature cannot be fully captured by one idea.

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: God as Law-Giver is most central to Jewish practice
data.targetWord: The concept of God as Law-Giver defines the Jewish people's unique relationship with God through Torah and mitzvot. This practical dimension — how to live — may be more central to Jewish life than theological concepts.

data.sourceWord: MCQ: How long does Yom Kippur fasting last?
data.targetWord: Twenty-five hours

examples.en-GB: Answer: Twenty-five hours | Distractors: Twelve hours; All day and night (24 hours); Three days

data.sourceWord: Yom Kippur — Day of Atonement
data.targetWord: Yom Kippur (Day of Atonement) is the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. Jews fast for 25 hours, attend synagogue for extended prayers including Kol Nidre, and seek God's forgiveness for sins of the past year.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q2.2 — importance of Yom Kippur

data.sourceWord: Yom Kippur — repentance and reconciliation
data.targetWord: Before Yom Kippur, Jews must seek forgiveness from any person they have wronged — God can only forgive sins against him, not against others. The day culminates in the Neilah service and the blowing of the shofar.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q2.2 — importance of Yom Kippur

data.sourceWord: Rosh Hashanah — Jewish New Year
data.targetWord: Rosh Hashanah (Jewish New Year) begins the Ten Days of Awe leading to Yom Kippur. The shofar (ram's horn) is blown as a call to repentance, and Jews eat apples and honey for a sweet new year.

data.sourceWord: Rosh Hashanah contrasted with Yom Kippur
data.targetWord: Rosh Hashanah is a day of celebration and hope for the new year, while Yom Kippur ten days later is solemn and penitential. Together they form the High Holy Days, the most spiritually serious period of the year.

data.sourceWord: Shabbat — the day of rest
data.targetWord: Shabbat (Saturday) is the weekly day of rest commanded in the Torah. Observant Jews light candles, recite Kiddush over wine, attend synagogue, and refrain from the 39 categories of forbidden work.

data.sourceWord: Shabbat — spiritual renewal and family
data.targetWord: Shabbat provides a weekly opportunity for prayer, Torah study, family time, and spiritual renewal. It commemorates both God's rest at creation and the Jewish people's liberation from slavery in Egypt.

data.sourceWord: Scripture: Shabbat commanded in the Torah
data.targetWord: 'Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy. Six days you shall labour and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God.' (Exodus 20:8-10)

data.sourceWord: FOR: Yom Kippur is most important — reconciliation with God
data.targetWord: Yom Kippur is described as the holiest day in Judaism. Through fasting and prayer Jews are 'sealed' in the Book of Life for another year. No other practice so directly addresses the human-divine relationship.

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: Shabbat is observed every week — more central
data.targetWord: Shabbat is observed every week for the entire Jewish community, making it the most regular and pervasive religious practice. Its weekly rhythm shapes Jewish life more consistently than any annual festival.

data.prompt: What is the Messiah in Orthodox Judaism?
data.answer: The Messiah is an individual who will come and bring peace.
Yom Kippur is the Day of Atonement and the holiest day in Judaism.
Shabbat commemorates God's rest at creation and freedom from slavery.

data.title: The High Holy Days in Judaism
data.sourceTitle: The High Holy Days in Judaism
data.sourcePassage: The High Holy Days (Yamim Nora'im — 'Days of Awe') are the most spiritually significant period in the Jewish calendar. They begin with Rosh Hashanah (the Jewish New Year) and end ten days later with Yom Kippur (the Day of Atonement). Rosh Hashanah is a day of celebration and reflection. The shofar (ram's horn) is blown to call the community to repentance. Jews eat apples dipped in honey to symbolise hopes for a sweet new year, and attend synagogue for extended prayers. Jewish tradition teaches that on Rosh Hashanah God opens the Book of Life and begins to judge each person's deeds from the past year. The ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are used for reflection and seeking forgiveness from those one has wronged. Yom Kippur itself is a day of fasting, prayer and confession. Jews spend much of the day in synagogue, reciting confessional prayers and asking God for forgiveness. The day ends with the Neilah (closing) service and a final, long blast of the shofar, after which Jews break their fast.
